title: A 27-year-old male patient presents to your clinic for an initial examination. He reports he just moved to New York from Washington, so he needs a new dentist. The patient reports he had four radiographs taken one year ago at his previous dentist but does not remember which type. You call the patient's previous dental office, and the previous office says they will mail you all of his radiographs as soon as possible. On intraoral examination, the patient's dentition has gross carious decay and multiple failing restorations. The gingiva looks red and inflamed. What radiographs should you take at today's dental appointment?
Oral Radiology Midterm Exam (Fall 2018): Bitewing radiographs only since you should take bitewings every 6 months
oralrad: Full mouth series because of the patient's high-risk category
midterm: No radiographs today; wait for the previous radiographs to arrive by mail to decide if new radiographs are needed
column5: Periapical radiographs only since you should take periapicals every 6 months

title: A 30-year-old female patient, 8 months pregnant, presents to your clinic for comprehensive dental care. The patient denies any pain or discomfort although she was told she has “pregnancy gingivitis.” On intraoral examination, you see that her gingiva is a bit swollen throughout her mouth. The patient reports she has never had dental radiographs taken. Which of the following is the most appropriate radiographic prescription?
Oral Radiology Midterm Exam (Fall 2018): Take a single periapical radiograph of the tooth that hurts the most.
oralrad: Take a full mouth series of radiographs.
column5: Defer taking any radiographs for about one month until the patient is no longer pregnant.
